hints: Think about what happens when a reaction creates a chiral centre without any chiral influence, do you get one mirror image or both in equal amounts?
walkthrough:
Picture the two mirror images**
Think of your left and right hands. Optical isomers (enantiomers) are like that, non-superimposable mirror images that rotate plane polarised light in opposite directions by the same amount.

Link equal amounts to no net rotation**
When both are present in exactly a 50:50 ratio, their rotations cancel out. That 50:50 mixture is what we call racemic, and it is optically inactive.
Final answer: A mixture containing equal amounts of the two optical isomers / enantiomers.

hints: Look at Fig. 6.1 and count how many carbon atoms are in different bonding environments, and group protons by their neighbouring atoms.
walkthrough:
Count carbon environments**
Look at $\text{H}_{2}\text{NCO-CH}_{2}\text{-CH(NH}_{2}\text{)-COOH}$. There are four carbons and all four are different: amide $\text{C=O}$, $\text{CH}_{2}$, chiral $\text{CH}$, and acid $\text{C=O}$. No symmetry makes any two the same, so $^{13}$C NMR shows 4 peaks.

Count proton environments in $\text{CDCl}_{3}$**
In this non-aqueous solvent exchangeable $\text{N-H}$ and $\text{O-H}$ protons are seen. Group them: amide $\text{NH}_{2}$, $\text{CH}_{2}$, chiral $\text{CH}$, amine $\text{NH}_{2}$, acid $\text{OH}$. That gives 5 distinct proton environments, so $^{1}$H NMR shows 5 peaks.
Final answer: carbon-13 NMR: 4 peaks; proton ($^{1}$H) NMR: 5 peaks.

hints: Recall that an amino acid can be cationic at low pH, anionic at high pH, and somewhere in between the positive and negative charges exactly balance.
walkthrough:
Think charge versus pH**
At very low pH both $\text{-NH}_{2}$ and $\text{-COOH}$ are protonated so the amino acid is positive. At very high pH both are deprotonated so it is negative. In between there must be a pH where $\text{-NH}_{3}^{+}$ and $\text{-COO}^{-}$ balance.

Name that balance point**
That pH is the isoelectric point. The molecule is mainly present as the zwitterion $\text{H}_{3}\text{N}^{+}\text{-R-COO}^{-}$ with overall charge zero, so it does not move in electrophoresis.
Final answer: The pH at which the amino acid exists as a zwitterion / has no overall charge.

hints: At pH 1.0, well below the isoelectric point of 5.4, decide whether $\text{-COOH}$ and $\text{-NH}_{2}$ will be protonated or deprotonated, remembering the side chain amide is not basic.
walkthrough:
Apply very acidic conditions**
At pH 1.0 you have a large excess of $\text{H}^{+}$. Both the alpha amino group and the alpha carboxyl group will be fully protonated. So $\text{-NH}_{2}$ becomes $\text{-NH}_{3}^{+}$ and $\text{-COO}^{-}$ becomes $\text{-COOH}$.

Leave the side chain alone**
The side chain is $\text{-CH}_{2}\text{-C(=O)-NH}_{2}$, a neutral amide. It is not protonated under these conditions. So you draw $\text{H}_{2}\text{N-C(=O)-CH}_{2}\text{-CH(NH}_{3}^{+}\text{)-COOH}$, a singly positively charged cation.
Final answer: $\text{H}_{2}\text{N-C(=O)-CH}_{2}\text{-CH(NH}_{3}^{+}\text{)-C(=O)-OH}$ with the side chain amide $\text{CONH}_{2}$ unchanged.

hints: Recall that polymerisation of amino acids is condensation between $\text{-COOH}$ of one monomer and $\text{-NH}_{2}$ of the next, forming $\text{-CO-NH-}$ with loss of water.

Think about how to show two linked asparagine residues with the side chain $\text{-CH}_{2}\text{CONH}_{2}$ untouched and the peptide link displayed as $\text{-C(=O)-N(H)-}$ with continuation bonds at each end.
walkthrough:
Form the peptide link**
Join the $\text{C=O}$ from the acid end of one asparagine to the $\text{NH}$ from the amine end of the next. Water is lost and you get the amide link $\text{-C(=O)-N(H)-}$. You must display it, meaning draw out $\text{C=O}$ and $\text{N-H}$ atoms, not just a line.

Build two repeat units correctly**
Each repeat unit is $\text{-NH-CH(R)-CO-}$ where $\text{R = CH}_{2}\text{-C(=O)-NH}_{2}$. The side chain amide stays unchanged. Put continuation bonds through the ends to show the chain continues, like $\text{-NH-CH(R)-C(=O)-NH-CH(R)-C(=O)-}$.

Final answer: Two asparagine residues linked by displayed peptide bond: $\text{-[NH-CH(CH}_{2}\text{CONH}_{2}\text{)-C(=O)]-[NH-CH(CH}_{2}\text{CONH}_{2}\text{)-C(=O)]-}$ with continuation bonds at both ends and $\text{-C(=O)-NH-}$ shown displayed.

hints: Compare buffer pH 5.0 with the isoelectric points, asn 5.4 and lys 9.8, to decide which species will be essentially neutral and which will be positively charged.
Recall that in electrophoresis cations move toward the negative electrode, and a neutral zwitterion stays near the origin.
For the two cations, consider which has the larger $M_{r}$ and therefore moves more slowly through the support medium.
walkthrough:
Work out the charge at pH 5.0**
Buffer pH 5.0 is just below the pI of asparagine (5.4), so asn is almost a neutral zwitterion with only a tiny positive charge. It barely moves, so spot E at the origin is Asn. Buffer pH is well below the pI of lysine (9.8), so lysine is fully protonated and positively charged. The dipeptide lys-asn will also carry that extra lysine $\text{-NH}_{3}^{+}$ group and be positive.

Decide direction of movement**
Positive ions migrate toward the negative electrode on the right in Fig. 6.3. That matches spots F and G which have moved to the right, while E has stayed. So F and G are the two positive species, Lys and Lys-Asn.

Use size to split F and G**
Both F and G are cations, but Lys-Asn is a dipeptide with much larger $M_{r}$ than free Lys. Larger ions experience more friction and migrate more slowly. So the nearer spot F is the bulkier Lys-Asn, and the furthest spot G is the smaller, faster Lys.

Final answer: E: Asn; F: Lys-Asn; G: Lys.
At pH 5.0, Lys and Lys-Asn are positively charged and move toward the negative electrode, while Asn (pI 5.4) is nearly uncharged and stays at E near the origin.
Lys-Asn has the highest $M_{r}$ so moves the shorter distance to F, Lys moves furthest to G.

hints: Remember TLC uses a solid coated on a plate while GLC sweeps the sample through with a gas.
walkthrough:
Match phase to technique**
In TLC the stationary phase is the solid thin layer, typically silica gel or aluminium oxide on a glass or plastic plate. In GLC the mobile phase is the unreactive carrier gas, such as nitrogen or helium, that carries vapourised sample through the liquid-coated column.
Final answer: thin-layer chromatography stationary phase: aluminium oxide / silica (on solid support); gas-liquid chromatography mobile phase: inert gas e.g. $\text{N}_{2}$ / He / Ar.

hints: Look for the reference spot that lines up vertically with the unknown in solvent 1 and check if the same match holds in solvent 2.
walkthrough:
Compare spots in both solvents**
In solvent 1 the unknown at about 1.7 cm matches Q and S, but in solvent 2 the unknown at about 3.7 cm matches only R and S. The only reference that coincides in both runs is S. A single solvent match could be coincidence, identical $R_{f}$ in two different solvents confirms identity, so the unknown is S.
Final answer: S, because its $R_{f}$ value matches the unknown amino acid in both solvents.

hints: Use the peak areas to scale the known mass concentration of K to find the mass concentration of L, then divide by $M_{r}$ of L to get mol $\text{dm}^{-3}$.
walkthrough:
Scale by peak area to get mass concentration**
Peak area is proportional to mass present. So: $$\text{mass conc. of L} = \frac{\text{area L}}{\text{area K}} \times \text{mass conc. of K} = \frac{58}{44} \times 5.52 \times 10^{-2} = 7.28 \times 10^{-2} \text{ g dm}^{-3}$$
Step 2: **Convert mass to moles**
Divide by $M_{r}$ of L, 116: $$c = \frac{7.28 \times 10^{-2}}{116} = 6.27 \times 10^{-4} \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$$ Keep at least 2 significant figures with units $\text{mol dm}^{-3}$.
Final answer: mass conc. of L $= 58/44 \times 5.52 \times 10^{-2} = 7.28 \times 10^{-2}$ $\text{g dm}^{-3}$; conc. of L $= 7.28 \times 10^{-2} / 116 = 6.27 \times 10^{-4}$ $\text{mol dm}^{-3}$.
